blocks.text: Every linked list is a chain of nodes joined by pointers. What changes between the **three types** is **which pointers each node has** and **where the last node points**. That one choice decides which directions you can walk, what each operation costs and what the list is good for.

blocks.alt: The three types side by side. Singly linked: 10, 20, 30, each pointing forward, ending in null. Doubly linked: the same values, each node pointing forward to the next and back to the previous, with null at both ends. Circular: 10, 20, 30 pointing forward, and the last node's arrow curving back to the first node instead of to null.

blocks.text: Each node holds a value and **one pointer**, `next`. You start at the **head** and can only move **forward**; the last node's `next` is **null**. It is the simplest and lightest type, and the one most interview questions use — every lesson so far has been about it.

items: **Walk forward:** yes. **Walk backward:** no — a node doesn't know what comes before it.
**Delete a node:** you need the node **before** it (to fix its `next`), so deleting a node you're pointing at means searching from the head: O(n).

blocks.text: Each node holds a value and **two pointers**: `next` to the node after it and `prev` to the node before it. The head's `prev` and the tail's `next` are null. Because every node knows both neighbours, you can walk **in both directions**, and you can unlink a node you're holding in **O(1)** — no search for its predecessor.

blocks.alt: One doubly linked node close up: a box split into three parts. The left part holds the prev pointer, the middle the value 20, and the right part the next pointer. Arrows show prev pointing back to the node before and next pointing on to the node after.

blocks.text: The price is **one more pointer per node** (8 bytes on a 64-bit machine) and **twice the pointer updates** on every insert and delete — forget one and the two directions disagree. Real libraries use doubly linked lists: Java's `LinkedList`, C++'s `std::list` and Python's `collections.deque` (blocks linked both ways).

The last node's `next` points **back to the first node** instead of to null. There is no end: from any node you can reach every other node, and a walk that doesn't stop on purpose goes round forever. A circular list is usually held by its **tail** rather than its head — `tail.next` **is** the head, so both ends are one step away and adding at either end is O(1).

A circular list can also be **doubly linked**: the head's `prev` points to the tail and the tail's `next` to the head. Operating systems schedule processes round-robin on such rings, and music players use one for **repeat all**.

blocks.alt: A comparison table. Pointers per node: singly has next; doubly has prev and next; circular has next, with the tail pointing to the head. Walk backwards: no, yes, no. Where the list ends: at null, at null in both directions, never. Delete a node you are holding: O(n), O(1), O(n). Extra memory: none, one pointer per node, none. Typical uses: stacks and hash buckets; browser history and LRU caches; round-robin turns and playlists on repeat.

items: **Singly** when you only ever move forward: stacks, queues, hash table buckets, and almost every interview question that just says **linked list**.
**Doubly** when you need to go **back**, or to remove items from the **middle** quickly once you've found them: browser back/forward, undo/redo, LRU caches, text editors.
**Circular** when the data is a **loop** by nature — turns in a game, round-robin scheduling, a playlist on repeat — or when you want O(1) access to both ends from one tail pointer.
**Singly**: `next` only, forward only, ends at null. The lightest and the most common.
**Doubly**: `prev` and `next`, walks both ways, unlinks a held node in O(1) — at the cost of one more pointer per node and more pointers to update.
**Circular**: the tail points back to the head, so there's no null to stop at. Keep a tail pointer and both ends are O(1).
The next lessons show how to **traverse**, insert and delete in all three types, and the interview questions are grouped by type.
